hook.situation: A plan changes while you are on the way, eating, watching something, or already seated somewhere.
objectives: Use V-다가 when an action is interrupted, paused, or changed mid-way.
Use V-아/어 있다 for a state that remains after an action or change.
Explain changed plans with practical words like 중간에, 바꾸다, 취소하다, 문자, and 갑자기.
hook.whyItMatters: English 'while' can hide the difference between two actions happening together and one action being interrupted. Korean -다가 clearly says the first action was in progress and then something changed. V-아/어 있다 then lets you describe the state after the change.

grammarNotes.title: V-다가 - while doing, then something changes
grammarNotes.mentalModel: -다가 catches the moment where action 1 is in progress and the situation turns.
grammarNotes.formation: Attach -다가 directly to the verb stem: 가다 becomes 가다가, 먹다 becomes 먹다가, 보다 becomes 보다가, 공부하다 becomes 공부하다가. The first action is not presented as fully finished. It is interrupted, paused, changed, or becomes the background for what happens next.

examples.en: I got a phone call while I was on my way to school.
examples.note: Going was in progress when the call came.

examples.en: A call came while I was eating.
examples.note: The meal is interrupted or at least paused.

examples.en: I fell asleep while watching the movie.
examples.note: The watching did not smoothly finish first.

examples.en: I studied, then took a short break in the middle.
examples.note: A temporary switch away from studying.

b.en: I left while eating / before finishing.

contrastPairs.explanation: -고 나서 says the first action finished. -다가 says the first action was cut into.

a.en: I study while listening to music.

b.en: I was studying, then switched to listening to music.

contrastPairs.explanation: -(으)면서 means simultaneous actions. -다가 means a switch or interruption.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Do not put past tense inside the first verb for ordinary -다가. The later clause carries the tense.

exceptions: In casual Korean, -다가 can shorten to -다: 집에 가다 전화 받았어.
A different event can interrupt the first action: 밥을 먹다가 전화가 왔어요.
If action 1 really finished before action 2, use -고 나서 instead.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 있다 - the resulting state remains
grammarNotes.mentalModel: V-아/어 있어요 shows the state left after something happened: sitting, standing, open, closed, on, or placed.
grammarNotes.formation: Use the 아/어 form plus 있다: 앉다 becomes 앉아 있어요, 서다 becomes 서 있어요, 열리다 becomes 열려 있어요, 켜지다 becomes 켜져 있어요. The subject is usually the thing or person in the state, often with 이/가 or a location with 에.

examples.en: I am sitting at the cafe.
examples.note: The action of sitting down is done; the seated state remains.
The door opened and remains open.
The light turned on and remains on.
서 있어요 describes the standing state.

a.en: I am in the act of sitting down.

contrastPairs.explanation: -고 있어요 is the action in progress. -아/어 있어요 is the resulting state.
Transitive action uses 을/를. Result state usually makes the thing the subject with 이/가.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: For result state, the door is the subject of the state. Use 이/가, not 을/를.

exceptions: Do not use -아/어 있다 with ordinary ongoing actions like eating or reading. Say 먹고 있어요, 읽고 있어요.
Many useful result-state verbs are intransitive or passive-like: 열리다, 닫히다, 켜지다.
앉아 있어요 and 서 있어요 are extremely common status sentences.

exampleSentence.en: I got a call while going to school.
exampleSentence.note: 가다가 is the core movement interruption frame.

exampleSentence.en: A call came while I was eating.
exampleSentence.note: The meal is not the completed first step.

exampleSentence.en: I fell asleep while watching the movie.

exampleSentence.note: The object being changed takes 을/를.
A common reason a plan changes mid-way.

exampleSentence.en: I got a class cancellation text.
exampleSentence.note: The message interrupts the original plan.

exampleSentence.en: I got a text while riding the subway.
exampleSentence.note: -고 있다가 makes the ongoing ride explicit.
The incoming call can interrupt an action.

exampleSentence.en: I am sitting at the cafe.
exampleSentence.note: 앉아 있다 is a result-state phrase.
서 있다 describes a continuing posture or line state.

extendedVocabulary.english: to turn on; to be on

exampleSentence.en: The door is in an open state.
I suddenly got a text while going.
I will rest a little and then go again.

extendedDialogue.setting: A class is canceled while someone is already on the way.

readingText.title: A plan changes on the way
readingText.body: 지훈은 학교에 가다가 수업 취소 문자를 받았어요. 처음에는 그냥 학교까지 가려고 했지만, 지하철을 타고 있다가 문자를 보고 중간에 계획을 바꿨어요. 그래서 근처 카페로 갔어요. 카페 문이 열려 있었고 불도 켜져 있었어요. 지훈은 창가 자리에 앉아 있었어요. 조금 쉬다가 다시 집에 돌아가기로 했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Jihoon got a class cancellation text while going to school. At first he planned to keep going, but while riding the subway he saw the text and changed the plan midway. So he went to a nearby cafe. The cafe door was open and the light was on. Jihoon was sitting by the window. After resting a bit, he decided to go back home.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 카페는 어떤 상태였어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 문이 열려 있었고 불도 켜져 있었어요.

culturalNote.title: Explaining changed plans
culturalNote.body: When Korean speakers explain a changed plan, -다가 is very useful because it shows the original action was already underway. It sounds more natural than simply listing two past actions.
culturalNote.tip: Use -다가 for the interrupted action, then give the new result: 학교에 가다가 문자를 받고 카페로 갔어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence shows a mid-action interruption?
inlineExercises.explanation: -다가 shows the phone call happened while the first action was underway.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence describes the continuing state after sitting?
inlineExercises.explanation: 앉아 있어요 means the person is seated. The place takes 에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means the door is already open?
inlineExercises.explanation: Result state uses the thing as subject: 문이.
먹다가 shows the call interrupted the meal.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 불을 켜져 있어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: For result state, the light is the subject with 이/가.

bullets: V-다가 shows an action was interrupted or changed mid-way: 학교에 가다가 전화를 받았어요.
V-아/어 있어요 describes a continuing result state: 카페에 앉아 있어요, 문이 열려 있어요.
Use -다가, not -고 나서, when the first action did not simply finish before the second.
Result-state sentences usually make the thing or person in the state the subject: 문이, 불이, 사람이.
